newsitem.title: USA: CFTC: Prudential failed to supervise employee.
newsitem.headline: CFTC: Prudential failed to supervise employee.

text.p: Federal regulators Tuesday charged Prudential Securities Inc with failing to adequately supervise an employee and his two assistants who allegedly cheated customers in the trading of orange juice futures contracts.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission said it filed a four-count administrative complaint against Prudential and Kevin Marshburn, Kathryn Sarabasa and Kathleen Chiappone of central Florida.

The complaint charged Marshburn with violating federal commodities laws by "cheating, defrauding and deciving customers" in orange juice futures trading on the New York Cotton Exchange between May 1993 and March 1994.
The CFTC said Marshburn gave himself better prices on specific trades while giving customers worse prices, and failing to keep required records.

The complaint also alleged that Prudential violated federal commodities laws by failing to properly supervise Marshburn and failing to keep certain records. The agency complaint did not accuse Prudential of fraud.

Prudential said it "took appropriate steps" in investigating Marshburn's trading activities. "We spotted a possible issue with his trading, launched an investigation and then reported the investigation when the broker left the firm," Prudential said in a statement. "Our oversight procedures are in accordance with industry standards."

Marshburn and his assistants resigned to join another firm during Prudential's investigation of him, the brokerage firm. The trio of former Prudential employees were also charged with aiding and abetting Prudential's alleged recordkeeping violations. Chiappone and Sarabasa were also accused of order preparation and recordkeeping violations.

Under federal law, the CFTC must schedule a public hearing on the allegations and to determine what punishment, if any, should be imposed. Possible agency sanctions include civil penalties of up to $100,000 for each violation of commodities law, suspension of registration, prohibition of trading or cease and desist orders.
The CFTC has previously accused Refco and Merrill Lynch of failing to properly supervise employees.
